subject: Proposal: Spillover Settlement Framework for Reserved GPU Pools
messages:
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwood.com>

Subject: Proposal: Spillover Settlement Framework for Reserved GPU Pools

Hi Elena / Parcellytics team,

Thanks for the call earlier — based on the usage patterns you shared (short daytime surges tied to batch processing), we've sketched a proposal that keeps your reserved throughput predictable while giving limited, predictable breathing room for bursts. High-level components: 

- Soft-throttle window (grace): allow short bursts above commit for up to 60 minutes spread across a 24h sliding window before a hard throttle applies.
- Surge credits: monthly pool of credits (tokens) that convert to allocated GPU-seconds; unused credits rollover up to one month.
- Metering windows: 1-minute and 10-minute windows to determine transient vs sustained overruns.
- Settlement: sustained overrun beyond credits billed at a discounted overage rate with an automated true-up invoice.
- Reporting & alerting: hourly usage alerts and a daily spike summary; API access to per-model token and latency breakdowns.

I've attached a short term sheet with examples and a spreadsheet with sample math for your QPS/throughput bands. The document outlines three sample tiers for a 100-GPU reserved pool and how the credit bucket behaves under different patterns.

Attachments: [Attachment: RJ_Dedicated_Spillover_Terms_v1.pdf (pdf)], [Attachment: spillover_pricing_model.xlsx (xlsx)]

Key asks from you:
- Confirm whether a 60-minute grace across a 24h window sounds acceptable.
- If yes, share an expected monthly peak (GPU-hours) for the busiest weekday so we can size the credit pool.
- Any procurement/legal constraints we should pre-empt (preferred billing cadence, PO process, e-signature).

If this direction looks good, Marissa will follow up with an example pricing schedule and draft clause language for your legal team.

Thanks,
Jordan Blake

Jordan, thanks — this is helpful and aligns with what we discussed. A few clarifying questions before we loop in procurement/legal: 

1) The 60-minute grace — is that continuous (one 60min burst) or cumulative (many small bursts summing to 60min)?
2) Example math: can you show a concrete scenario where we hit a large 3-hour spike (two sustained hours + one short peak) — what would we actually pay vs. being throttled?
3) Credits: how large would the monthly credit pool be for a 100-GPU committed pool under the "typical daytime spike" profile?

Procurement: our preferred cadence is monthly invoices; will Redwood accept a PO and net-30? Also, legal will want the exact clause language for the spillover pricing and any hard throttle thresholds.

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Date: 2026-11-23T08:05:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Proposal: Spillover Settlement Framework for Reserved GPU Pools

Elena — answering inline and adding concrete numbers.

1) Grace definition: cumulative across a rolling 24-hour window. That means you can have many short bursts that sum to 60 minutes before the hard throttle kicks in. We chose cumulative because your traffic patterns show many sub-10-minute spikes.

2) Three-hour example (100-GPU committed pool):
- Baseline: 100 GPUs committed, normal monthly hours = 30 days * 24h = 72,000 GPU-hours.
- Scenario: On a busy day you run an extra 3 hours at +40 GPUs.
  - First 60 minutes: consumes credit bucket (no overage billing).
  - Remaining 120 minutes: treated as sustained overrun -> billed at overage rate (discounted) or throttled depending on remaining credits.

Sample numbers (from the attached spreadsheet):
- Surge credit pool suggested: 3,000 GPU-minutes (~50 GPU-hours) per month for the 100-GPU tier (covers typical daytime variability).
- Overage rate (sustained): 0.65x of on-demand per GPU-hour (discount relative to pay-as-you-go) with automated monthly true-up.
- If credits exhausted mid-spike: soft-throttle to 80% of committed throughput for the remainder of the sustained period; not a hard cut — we allow degraded throughput to preserve job progress.

3) Credit sizing for your profile: based on the telemetry you shared last month, we recommend starting at 3,000 GPU-minutes with a one-time lookback after 30 days to adjust. I'll attach the specific sheet rows we used.

Procurement: Redwood can do monthly invoices and accept a PO; standard payment terms are net-30 but we can discuss net-45 for larger contracts. Legal: attaching suggested clause language; happy to iterate.

Action items:
- Elena: approve the 3,000 GPU-minute credit baseline or provide an alternate target by EOD Friday.
- Jordan/Marissa: we'll produce a one-page contractual addendum and share with your legal.
- Aditya: any technical caveats on throttling behavior?

Best,
Marissa Cole

Subject: Re: Proposal: Spillover Settlement Framework for Reserved GPU Pools

Quick technical note on throttling and SLOs so procurement/legal knows what to expect operationally.

- Soft-throttle behavior: when credits are depleted and sustained overrun continues, we reduce per-request concurrency (not model quality) to target ~80% of committed throughput. That reduces queueing and tail latency while letting long-running batches progress.
- Fallbacks: during sustained pressure we can route non-critical traffic to a cheaper quantized model variant or lower-cost region if policy permits (this is optional and must be included in the rollout config).
- Metering: billing windows use our 1-minute sampled utilization combined into a 10-minute rolling average to determine whether usage is transient or sustained. This avoids billing short-lived spikes.
- Instrumentation: we will expose an endpoint for your SREs to pull per-GPU utilization and credit-bucket state; we recommend an alert when credits hit 50% and 90%.

Operational caveats: any hard throttling will be explicitly listed as an exceptional failover and requires a joint runbook for major incidents.

- Aditya
